entries.value: As of now, no country has approved BPC-157 as a prescription drug. It's not available through legitimate pharmacies for medical use. The peptide is officially designated for research use only.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken action against companies marketing BPC-157 as a dietary supplement, stating it does not meet the definition of a legal supplement ingredient. There is also no legal basis for compounding pharmacies to include BPC-157 in medications, though regulatory agencies have found some clinics doing so illegally.

Any product being sold is unregulated. Many websites sell BPC-157 as a "research chemical" with disclaimers that it's not for human use. This grey market means quality control is questionable – products might not contain the stated dose or could have impurities.

WADA has banned BPC-157 for athletes under the class of "S0: Non-approved substances." This means athletes can face sanctions if caught using it in sport. The ban signals that BPC-157 is considered experimental and not recognized as a legitimate medication.
One attractive feature of BPC-157 in research is its apparently favorable safety profile in animals. Toxicology studies have found no lethal dose even at extremely high amounts:
In rats, a single injection of 20 mg per kilogram (a massive dose for a peptide) caused no deaths or obvious toxic effects
In dogs, daily injections for a month at doses up to 1 mg/kg showed no significant adverse effects compared to control animals
Studies reported no changes in body weight, behavior, or organ health attributable to BPC-157

The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published as of 19 October 2026. In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and compounding: an advisory committee vote in July and an interim policy sent for White House review in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or makes it lawful to compound.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) met on 23–24 July 2026. On 23 July it considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the list of bulk drug substances that may be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the "503A Bulks List"). FDA evaluated both forms for ulcerative colitis. FDA's published voting questions were: "Should BPC-157 (free base) be placed on the list?" and "Should BPC-157 acetate be placed on the list?" In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither BPC-157 (free base) nor BPC-157 acetate be included on the 503A Bulks List. FDA states that advisory committee recommendations are non-binding. Reuters reported on 15 October 2026 that the advisers had recommended FDA loosen restrictions on six of the seven peptides reviewed in July, including BPC-157. As of 19 October 2026, FDA has not posted official minutes or vote tallies on the meeting page, so this entry gives no vote counts. The 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23) has not been amended to include BPC-157.

Interim access policy under OIRA review (received 14 October 2026). OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) lists a pending Executive Order 12866 review with these details (reginfo.gov, checked 19 October 2026; status "Pending EO 12866 Regulatory Review"). Title: "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides". Agency/Subagency: HHS / FDA. RIN: 0910-ZD94. Stage: Notice. Received Date: 10/14/2026. Legal Deadline: None. Economically Significant: No. The listing does not name any peptides and does not include the policy text. As of 19 October 2026, no matching Federal Register document and no FDA press announcement were found. Reuters, citing an Associated Press report based on two unnamed people, reported that the policy would allow some popular peptides, including BPC-157, to be compounded. That is a press report and has not been confirmed in any published text. Reginfo.gov lists three EO 12866 meetings on this review, on 21, 23 and 27 October 2026 (checked 22 October 2026); the 21 October meeting was requested by the American Academy of Peptide Medicine. EO 12866 meetings let outside parties present their views to OIRA while a review is pending; a scheduled meeting is not a decision and does not indicate the outcome.
Not an approval: neither the PCAC vote nor the OIRA submission is FDA approval of BPC-157 for any use.
No published text: the policy text has not been released, and no Federal Register notice has been located.
No effective or start date: none has been announced.
Scope unknown: the OIRA listing does not say which peptides would be covered.
Review is not a final policy: an OIRA review is a step before publication. The policy may be changed, withdrawn, or published in a different form.

old_value: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (15 amino acids) originally discovered in human gastric juice, with remarkable stability in harsh environments like stomach acid.
Preclinical research demonstrates significant healing potential for tendons, ligaments, muscles, bones, and gastrointestinal tissues through multiple biological pathways.
The peptide operates through pleiotropic mechanisms, increasing pro-healing factors (VEGF, nitric oxide) while decreasing inflammatory markers (COX-2, IL-6, TNF-α).
Human clinical evidence remains limited, with only small pilot studies conducted; BPC-157 is currently designated for research use only and is not approved by regulatory agencies.
The World Anti-Doping Agency has banned BPC-157 as a non-approved substance, and the FDA does not recognize it as a legal dietary supplement or drug ingredient.
key_points.new_item: Regulatory status (as of 19 Oct 2026): FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted on BPC-157 on 23 July 2026; the vote is non-binding. HHS/FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to OIRA on 14 Oct 2026. No text has been published, no effective date has been set, and coverage is unknown. This is not an approval.

old_value.question: How long does it take to see results from BPC-157?
old_value.answer: Most users report noticeable improvements in pain and mobility within 1-2 weeks. Full healing benefits may take 4-6 weeks depending on the severity of the injury.

old_value.question: Should I inject BPC-157 near the injury site?
old_value.answer: While systemic (anywhere) injection works, many users prefer injecting near the injury site for potentially faster local effects. Research suggests both methods are effective.

old_value.question: Can I take BPC-157 orally?
old_value.answer: Yes, but oral bioavailability is significantly lower than injection. For gut-related issues, oral administration may be beneficial. For musculoskeletal issues, injection is preferred.

new_value.question: Has BPC-157 been tested in humans?
new_value.answer: Only in a few very small studies. A 2026 systematic review (Poolton et al., Acta Orthopaedica Belgica; PMID 42885452) found three human studies with 30 participants in total: a retrospective chart review of knee pain (16 people), a retrospective pilot study in interstitial cystitis (12 people) and a two-person safety pilot. None had a control group. The reviewers judged all three to be of poor methodological quality and rated the overall certainty of evidence as very low. These studies cannot show whether BPC-157 is effective or safe in people.

new_value.question: What does the animal research on BPC-157 show?
new_value.answer: Most BPC-157 research is preclinical, mainly in rats. A 2025 systematic review (Vasireddi et al., HSS Journal; PMID 40756949) included 36 studies, 35 of them preclinical, and reported improved healing outcomes in animal models of muscle, tendon, ligament and bone injury. Many of these animal studies come from the University of Zagreb group led by Predrag Sikiric, which first described BPC-157 in 1993 (McGuire et al., 2025; PMID 40789979). They are developer-affiliated, and readers should weigh them with that in mind. Animal results do not show that the same effects occur in people.

new_value.question: Is BPC-157 approved by FDA or allowed in compounding?
new_value.answer: No. BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and as of 22 October 2026 it is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23). FDA's page on bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks lists BPC-157 in its "nominated but withdrawn" table (substances previously in Category 2), not on the current Category 2 list, and the page still describes FDA's safety concerns. On 23 July 2026 a narrow majority of FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, according to press reports, voted to recommend adding BPC-157 to the 503A Bulks List. The vote is non-binding, and FDA has not posted minutes. A separate HHS/FDA "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" (RIN 0910-ZD94) is under OIRA review at the Notice stage. Its text has not been published, and it is not an approval.

new_value.question: Is BPC-157 prohibited in sport?
new_value.answer: Yes. BPC-157 is named as an example in class S0 (Non-approved substances) of the World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 Prohibited List. Substances in S0 are prohibited at all times, in and out of competition.

new_value.question: Does PeptideMap give dosing, route or usage advice for BPC-157?
new_value.answer: No. PeptideMap is a research-use-only (RUO) comparison and reference site. It does not give dosing, route, timing, cycling, stacking, storage or sourcing guidance, and nothing on this page is medical advice. Products sold as BPC-157 "research chemicals" are not FDA-regulated drugs, and their content and purity are not verified.
